```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE, fig.align = "center", out.width = "100%")
source("../../_shared/template/viscount_rmd_helpers.R")
library(jsonlite)

read_json_file <- function (arg0_path) {
  txt <- readLines(arg0_path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  fromJSON(paste(txt, collapse = "\n"), simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json_file("colonial_settlements_and_trading_posts.json5")
set_data <- read_json_file("colonial_settlements_and_trading_posts_settlements.json")
led_data <- read_json_file("colonial_settlements_and_trading_posts_source_ledger.json5")

clean_text <- function (arg0_s) {
  s <- gsub("&", "and", as.character(arg0_s), fixed = TRUE)
  s <- gsub("_", " ", s, fixed = TRUE)
  trimws(s)
}

fmt_yr <- function (arg0_y) {
  y <- as.numeric(arg0_y)
  if (y < 0) return(paste0(abs(round(y)), "BC"))
  return(paste0(round(y), "AD"))
}

fmt_coord <- function (arg0_coords) {
  lat <- as.numeric(arg0_coords[[1]])
  lon <- as.numeric(arg0_coords[[2]])
  lat_s <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lat), 2L), if (lat >= 0) " N" else " S")
  lon_s <- paste0(viscount_fmt_number(abs(lon), 2L), if (lon >= 0) " E" else " W")
  paste0(lat_s, ", ", lon_s)
}

set_list <- unname(set_data)
sett_peaks <- vapply(set_list, function (s) {
  if (is.null(s$population) || length(s$population) == 0) return(0)
  max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
}, numeric(1))

reg_short <- list(
  col_konkan_gujarat_goa = "Konkan-Gujarat-Goa",
  col_malabar_cochin = "Malabar Coast",
  col_coromandel_madras = "Coromandel Coast",
  col_bengal_hugli_ceylon = "Hugli-Bengal and Ceylon"
)

exc_list <- Filter(function (c) identical(c$status, "excluded") || identical(c$included, FALSE), led_data$candidates)
```

# Abstract

This gazetteer compiles geographic coordinates, administrative affiliations,
foundation chronologies and longitudinal demographic trajectories for 19.644
catalogued settlements across four maritime macro-regions in South Asia (1.316.175
km²) between 1498AD and 1757AD. The catalogued network links fortified naval
headquarters, open riverine and roadstead factory posts, textile artisan centres
and agrarian market towns into an integrated spatial hierarchy. By reconciling
contemporary company muster rolls, municipal tax surveys, parish baptismal
registers, official national censuses, multi-repository archaeological corpora and
regional historical monographs [@Habib1982Atlas; @Moosvi1987Economy;
@Hambly1982Towns; @ImperialGazetteer1908], this gazetteer establishes a consistent
spatial baseline for demographic disaggregation from the arrival of the Portuguese
at Calicut to the establishment of British territorial rule in Bengal.

The catalogued settlements reflect two and a half centuries of commercial contact
and urban nucleation across four macro-regions: the Konkan, Gujarat and Estado da
India littoral (5.551 settlements); the Malabar coast factories (3.043 settlements);
the Coromandel coast enclaves (4.474 settlements); and the Hugli-Bengal factories
alongside maritime Ceylon (6.576 settlements). While major maritime trading posts
such as Surat (200k peak in 1700AD), Chennai (Madras, 140k peak in 1757AD), Kolkata
(Calcutta, 115k in 1757AD), Velha Goa (95k peak in 1600AD) and Mumbai (Bombay, 85k
in 1757AD) anchored oceanic commercial flows, the largest demographic concentrations
resided within pre-colonial and regional capitals including Hampi (420k peak in
1500AD), Ahmedabad (240k peak in 1650AD), Vijayapura (220k peak in 1650AD), Gaur
(199,4k peak in 1500AD), Murshidabad (195k peak in 1750AD) and Aurangabad (165k
peak in 1700AD). Across the 19.644 settlements, the rank-size distribution fits a
Zipf power law of $\alpha = 0,91$ ($R^2 = 0,99$).

Every catalogued entry conforms to geographic inclusion standards. Localities possess
documented WGS84 coordinates, historical toponyms cross-referenced against early
modern European and Asian cartography, and validated population benchmarks derived
from primary-monograph trajectories, archaeological site surveys and national
censuses. All 19.644 entries reconcile with the 20.444-candidate source ledger
alongside 800 documented candidate exclusions (primarily spatial consolidations
within 3 km and non-residential toponyms), documenting the spatial distribution of
the 71,0M inhabitants of the maritime domain at 1757AD.

# Coastal Enclaves and Settlement Systems

Early modern urban systems along the Indian Ocean seaboard reflected structural
interactions between European commercial institutions and indigenous urban
traditions [@Malekandathil2020Maritime; @Pearson1971Commerce]. Four primary
settlement types characterised the maritime urban landscape:

1. Fortified Naval Enclaves: Typified by Velha Goa, Diu, Daman, Bassein, Fort
Manuel in Cochin, Fort Geldria in Pulicat, Fort St George in Madras, Fort William in
Calcutta, and Fort d'Orléans in Chandernagore [@Ames2000Renascent; @Forrest1908Siege].
These settlements combined heavy stone curtain walls, bastions and artillery batteries
with European administrative quarters, garrisons, dockyards and cathedrals,
exercising sovereign jurisdiction over immediately adjacent districts
[@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Abreu2020Health].

2. Riverine and Roadstead Factory Lodges: In major indigenous commercial ports such as
Surat, Bharuch, Masulipatnam and Hugli town, European trading nations maintained
unfortified commercial houses (*lodges*) under the authority of local governors,
coexisting within dense indigenous merchant quarters [@Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia;
@Arasaratnam1967Dutch]. These factories functioned as warehouses, residential
compounds and trading exchanges coordinating with native brokers (*dalals*) and
shroffs [@Pearson1971Commerce; @Clegg2017East].

3. Specialised Artisan and Weaver Hamlets: Distributed throughout coastal deltas
and river corridors, thousands of agricultural and manufacturing villages produced
export textiles under advance-contract systems (*dadni*). Settlements in the Cauvery,
Krishna-Godavari and lower Ganges deltas housed specialised castes of weavers,
bleachers and dyers who supplied cotton calicoes, muslins and chintz to European
purchasers [@Arasaratnam1967Dutch; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel].

4. Cinnamon and Spice Production Villages: Across maritime Ceylon and the Malabar
backwaters, rural settlements were organised around the compulsory harvesting of
cinnamon bark (*chalia* peelers under *rajakariya* service in Ceylon) and pepper
cultivation, integrating village agrarian structures with corporate export
monopolies [@WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing; @Lohuizen1961Dutch].

# Methodology and Source Ledger Reconciliation

The expanded 19.644-settlement gazetteer is empirically anchored rather than derived
from arbitrary scaling parameters. Candidate localities in the INDUS source ledger
were compiled and verified across four cumulative reconciliation waves linking
primary archival collections (Arquivo Historico Ultramarino, Nationaal Archief, and
the British Library Oriental and India Office Collections) with empirical spatial
corpora [@Ratcliff2025Monopolizi; @Embleton2023Names]:
- Wave 1 (11.394 settlements): Primary-monograph historical metropolis trajectories
[@Stein1989Vijayanagara; @Hambly1982Towns; @Eaton1993Rise; @Naqvi1968Urbanisation;
@Champakalakshmi1996Trade; @Moosvi1987Economy] and official national censuses,
principally Census of India Table A-04 sub-district series alongside PBS, BBS, DCS,
CBS, NSB and NBS registries and the Imperial Gazetteer of India
[@ImperialGazetteer1908].
- Wave 2 (5.500 settlements): Multi-repository archaeological and monument corpora,
combining Pleiades, Zenodo Harappan, Vidarbha and Palaeolithic Indian Archaeology
Reviews (IARs), Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) P1371 records, Wikidata,
OpenStreetMap (OSM) and XRONOS/c14bazAAR radiocarbon site catalogues
[@Allchin1995Archaeology; @Erdosy1988Urbanisation; @Chattopadhyaya1994Making;
@Possehl1999IndusAge; @Kenoyer1998AncientCities].
- Wave 3 (2.750 settlements): Macro-envelope *qasba*, *pargana* and *nadu*
continuity modelling grounded in Mughal and regional revenue geography
[@Habib1982Atlas; @Bayly1983Rulers], filtered by documented foundation years and
chronological toponymy rules so that post-1757AD foundations and anachronistic
colonial aliases are excluded.
- Wave 4 (0 marginal additions): Terminal submask gap-hunter and GeoNames homonym
sweep confirming complete spatial saturation across all four submasks.

Inclusion requires:
- Precise geographic coordinates referenced to the WGS84 datum.
- Documented early modern historical occupation spanning 1498AD to 1757AD verified
against foundation-year and chronological toponymy filters.
- Quantitative or narrative demographic evidence calibrated against primary
monographs, tax rolls, official census series or regional *qasba*/*nadu* densities,
yielding a Zipf rank-size fit of $\alpha = 0,91$ ($R^2 = 0,99$).

Table \ref{tab:summary} summarises the distribution of 19.644 catalogued settlements
and summed site peaks across the four macro-regions.

```{r tbl-summary, results='asis'}
sum_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function (rk) {
  sub_sets <- Filter(function (s) identical(s$region_id, rk) || identical(s$region, rk), set_list)
  peaks <- if (length(sub_sets) > 0) vapply(sub_sets, function (s) max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population))), numeric(1)) else 0
  top_name <- if (length(sub_sets) > 0) clean_text(sub_sets[[which.max(peaks)]]$name) else "-"
  top_pk <- if (length(sub_sets) > 0) max(peaks) else 0
  data.frame(
    SubRegion = reg_short[[rk]],
    Sites = viscount_fmt_number(length(sub_sets), 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(length(sub_sets) / length(set_list) * 100, 1L), "%"),
    PeakSum = viscount_fmt_pop(sum(peaks)),
    LeadingSite = paste0(top_name, " (", viscount_fmt_pop(top_pk), ")"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_sum <- do.call(rbind, sum_rows)
df_tot_sum <- data.frame(
  SubRegion = "Regional Total",
  Sites = viscount_fmt_number(length(set_list), 0L),
  Share = "100%",
  PeakSum = viscount_fmt_pop(sum(sett_peaks)),
  LeadingSite = paste0(clean_text(set_list[[which.max(sett_peaks)]]$name), " (", viscount_fmt_pop(max(sett_peaks)), ")"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
df_sum <- rbind(df_sum, df_tot_sum)
viscount_table(
  df_sum,
  "Macro-regional distribution of 19.644 catalogued settlements and summed site peaks across early modern South Asia.",
  c("Maritime Macro-Region", "Catalogued Sites", "Site Share", "Sum of Peaks", "Leading Settlement (Peak)"),
  list(label = "tab:summary", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Leading Early Modern Settlements and Trading Ports

Table \ref{tab:gazetteer} presents the leading 45 early modern settlements ordered by
peak population descending, detailing coordinates, macro-regional affiliation,
occupation span and benchmark demographic series.

```{r tbl-gazetteer, results='asis'}
ord_all <- order(sett_peaks, decreasing = TRUE)
top_45 <- set_list[ord_all[seq_len(min(45L, length(set_list)))]]

gaz_rows <- lapply(top_45, function (s) {
  yrs <- as.numeric(names(s$population))
  y_min <- min(yrs)
  y_max <- max(yrs)
  span_s <- if (y_min == y_max) fmt_yr(y_min) else paste0(fmt_yr(y_min), " - ", fmt_yr(y_max))
  pk <- max(as.numeric(unlist(s$population)))
  p_1757 <- if (!is.null(s$population[["1757"]])) as.numeric(s$population[["1757"]]) else "-"
  reg_lbl <- if (!is.null(s$region_id) && !is.null(reg_short[[s$region_id]])) reg_short[[s$region_id]] else if (!is.null(reg_short[[s$region]])) reg_short[[s$region]] else clean_text(s$region)
  data.frame(
    Settlement = substr(clean_text(s$name), 1, 24),
    SubRegion = reg_lbl,
    Coordinates = fmt_coord(s$coords),
    Span = span_s,
    Peak = viscount_fmt_pop(pk),
    P1757AD = if (is.numeric(p_1757)) viscount_fmt_pop(p_1757) else "-",
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_gaz <- do.call(rbind, gaz_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_gaz,
  "Leading 45 early modern settlements ordered by peak population across early modern India (1498AD to 1757AD).",
  c("Settlement Name", "Maritime Region", "Coordinates", "Span", "Peak Pop", "1757AD Pop"),
  list(label = "tab:gazetteer", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Macro-Regional Settlement Catalogues

## Konkan, Gujarat and Estado da India Littoral

The western maritime macro-region catalogues 5.551 settlements spanning Gujarat, the
Konkan coast and Goa [@Pearson1971Commerce; @Ames2000Renascent; @Habib1982Atlas].
Ahmedabad stood as the largest urban centre in the submask, peaking at 240k in
1650AD before moderating to 125k by 1757AD [@Hambly1982Towns; @Moosvi1987Economy].
Surat represented the premier maritime emporium of the Mughal Empire, peaking at
200k inhabitants in 1700AD (135k in 1757AD) with dense suburbs of weavers, shroffs
and Armenian traders [@Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia; @Aslanian2004Trade; @Hambly1982Towns].

Inland political and manufacturing hubs carried substantial weight: Aurangabad
peaked at 165k in 1700AD (95k in 1757AD), Burhanpur peaked at 135k in 1650AD (75k
in 1757AD) [@Naqvi1968Urbanisation], Ahmadnagar reached 104,9k in 1600AD, and Pune
expanded to 110k by 1757AD as the political seat of the Maratha Peshwas. Along the
coast, Khambhat peaked at 98,6k in 1498AD (35k in 1757AD), Velha Goa peaked at 95k
in 1600AD before declining to 12k in 1757AD [@Abreu2020Health; @Paiva2022Concord],
Vadodara reached 85k in 1757AD, Bharuch peaked at 55k in 1650AD, and Mumbai
(Bombay) expanded steadily from 10,5k in 1550AD and 15k in 1650AD to 45k in 1700AD
and 85k in 1757AD. Fortified coastal strongholds at Diu, Daman, Bassein and Chaul
commanded transit dues across the Gulf of Khambhat and Konkan waterways.

## Malabar Coast Factories

The Malabar coast catalogues 3.043 settlements along the southwest seaboard and its
interior plateau corridors [@Malekandathil2020Maritime; @degard2019Constructi].
Pre-colonial regional authority centred on Hampi (Vijayanagara), which reached 420k
inhabitants in 1500AD before contracting to 11,1k by 1600AD following the 1565AD
collapse [@Stein1989Vijayanagara], and on the Sultanate capital at Vijayapura
(Bijapur, 220k peak in 1650AD; 35k in 1757AD) alongside Bidar (93,5k peak in
1498AD). Along the immediate coastline, Kozhikode (Calicut, 75k peak in 1498AD; 50k
in 1757AD) functioned as the historic seat of the Zamorins, while Kochi (Cochin,
55k peak in 1600AD; 38k in 1757AD) housed Portuguese and Dutch naval shipyards
alongside Jewish and Christian commercial communities [@degard2019Constructi].

Additional coastal factories and interior centres included Srirangapatna (85k in
1757AD), Bengaluru (55k in 1757AD), Kollam (Quilon, 38,1k peak in 1498AD), Cannanore
(Fort St Angelo), French Mahé (founded 1721AD) and Thiruvananthapuram (48k in
1757AD), which expanded as the capital of Travancore under Marthanda Varma
[@Lohuizen1961Dutch].

## Coromandel Coast Enclaves

The Coromandel seaboard catalogues 4.474 settlements across Tamil Nadu and Andhra
Pradesh [@Arasaratnam1967Dutch; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel]. Chennai (Madras)
constituted the largest European Company metropolis, growing from 22k residents in
1650AD and 95k in 1700AD to 140k by 1757AD, organised into segregated White and
Black Towns [@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Clegg2017East]. Traditional dynastic and
temple centres retained large populations: Madurai (105k peak in 1650AD; 62k in
1757AD), Thanjavur (90k peak in 1650AD; 78k in 1757AD), Tiruchirappalli (82k peak in
1700AD; 78k in 1757AD), Arcot (75k peak in 1750AD; 65k in 1757AD) and Kanchipuram
(70,9k peak in 1500AD; 50k in 1757AD) [@Champakalakshmi1996Trade].

Commercial enclaves included the Golconda emporium of Machilipatnam (Masulipatnam,
100k peak in 1650AD; 65k in 1757AD), French Puducherry (Pondicherry, 58,9k peak in
1750AD; 55k in 1757AD), Dutch Nagapattinam (42k peak in 1700AD; 38k in 1757AD),
Dutch Fort Geldria at Pulicat (32k peak in 1650AD) and Danish Tharangambadi
(Tranquebar, 22k peak in 1700AD) [@Forrest1908Siege; @Subrahmanyam1989Coromandel;
@Kruijtzer2009Xenophobia]. Further south in the Gulf of Mannar, sacred chank and
pearl fisheries supported maritime settlements from Tuticorin to Rameswaram
[@Hornell1914Sacred].

## Hugli-Bengal Factories and Maritime Ceylon

The eastern macro-region catalogues 6.576 settlements across the lower Bengal delta
and the island of Ceylon [@Robins2012Corporatio; @WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing;
@Eaton1993Rise]. Pre-colonial and Nawabi capitals anchored the upper demographic
tier: Gaur reached 199,4k inhabitants in 1500AD, while Murshidabad peaked at 195k
in 1750AD (185k in 1757AD). Kolkata (Calcutta) expanded from 15k in 1700AD to 115k
inhabitants by 1757AD, flanked by Cuttack (79,5k peak in 1500AD), Hugli-Chinsurah
(72k peak in 1700AD; 55k in 1757AD), Natore (57,9k in 1757AD) and Bardhaman (52k in
1757AD).

Along the Hugli River, European competitors clustered within short distances: Dutch
Chinsurah, French Chandannagar (38k in 1757AD), Danish Serampore (12k in 1757AD)
and Portuguese Hugli. In maritime Ceylon, Colombo (42k in 1757AD) anchored Dutch
cinnamon collection, flanked by the fortified naval harbour at Galle, Jaffna,
Trincomalee and coastal peelers' villages [@Parthesius2010Dutch;
@WINTERBOTTOM2009Producing].

# Source Ledger Audit and Excluded Candidates

The INDUS source ledger records 20.444 candidates across the maritime domain. Of
these, 19.644 were included as catalogued settlements, while 800 entries were
excluded. Exclusions conform to systematic criteria:
1. Spatial deduplication (duplicate aliases): satellite survey coordinates and
suburban hamlets situated within 3 km of a primary nucleated settlement were
consolidated into the canonical record to prevent artificial clustering.
2. Non-residential toponyms: isolated lighthouses, offshore reefs, navigation
shoals and administrative divisions lacking permanent habitation were removed.

Table \ref{tab:excluded} documents the leading 25 excluded candidates alongside
their canonical primary settlement and justification.

```{r tbl-excluded, results='asis'}
exc_show <- exc_list[seq_len(min(25L, length(exc_list)))]
exc_rows <- lapply(exc_show, function (c) {
  j_txt <- clean_text(c$justification)
  if (nchar(j_txt) > 52) j_txt <- paste0(substr(j_txt, 1, 49), "...")
  data.frame(
    Candidate = substr(clean_text(c$name), 1, 24),
    Territory = clean_text(c$country),
    Reason = clean_text(c$reason),
    Justification = j_txt,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
df_exc <- do.call(rbind, exc_rows)
viscount_table(
  df_exc,
  "Leading twenty-five excluded candidate sites from the source ledger across the maritime domain.",
  c("Candidate Site", "Territory", "Exclusion Category", "Justification"),
  list(label = "tab:excluded", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

# Limitations and Preservation Biases

Historical demographic analysis of early modern Indian coastal settlements faces
specific taphonomic and documentary constraints:
1. Asymmetric Record Preservation: While European company archives document factory
personnel and trade values in detail, indigenous census data outside formal company
boundaries remain fragmentary [@Ratcliff2025Monopolizi; @Robins2012Corporatio].
2. Suburban and Transient Under-Enumeration: High seasonal mobility among weavers,
cart drivers and sailors produced substantial population turnover that was rarely
captured in static municipal rolls [@Chakrabarti2006Neither; @Rossum2019Labouring].
3. Fluvial and Geomorphological Change: Active siltation and channel migration along
the Hugli and deltaic rivers buried early modern wharf structures and shifted port
approaches over time [@Malekandathil2020Maritime].

Despite these constraints, reconciling 19.644 catalogued localities provides a
robust quantitative framework for early modern South Asian demographic history.
